title: Wi-Fi
objective: After this level you can explain how Wi-Fi uses radio waves to connect devices at home.
summary: Wi-Fi carries data by radio across the short hop between your devices and the router; the modem links your home to the provider. The 2.4 GHz band reaches farther, the 5 GHz band is faster.

cards.headline: "Wi-Fi" doesn't stand for anything.
cards.body: Not "wireless fidelity," whatever you've heard. A marketing firm picked the name because it sounded pleasant and echoed "hi-fi." The technology behind the catchy name is simpler than it sounds, and it covers only a tiny part of your data's journey.

cards.headline: The shortest hop of the trip
cards.body: Wi-Fi uses radio waves to move data over short distances, usually less than 100 meters indoors. Your router creates the home network and passes packets to and from each device by radio. A separate box, the modem, connects that network to your internet provider. So Wi-Fi covers only the few meters from your couch to the router. Everything after that is someone else's wires.

cards.headline: Two bands: reach or speed
cards.body: Most routers offer two bands. The 2.4 GHz band reaches farther and gets through walls better. The 5 GHz band is faster but covers a shorter range. A hertz is one cycle per second, and giga means billion, so 2.4 GHz waves swing back and forth 2.4 billion times a second. Remember Level 9's 60-hertz AC? Wi-Fi swings 40 million times faster.

cards.fact: Your laptop and a stranger's router work together because of a 1997 rulebook.
cards.context: That year the IEEE approved a common standard, 802.11, so equipment from different makers could connect. The group formed to promote it is now called the Wi-Fi Alliance, and its marketing firm is where the name "Wi-Fi" came from.
